title: How to Retire Without a Pension: A Complete U.S. Strategy
description: Building a 'Do-It-Yourself' pension using the 4% rule and annuities.
content:
Fifty years ago, retirement planning was simple: work for 30 years, get a gold watch, and collect a pension check until you die. Today, only ~15% of private-sector workers have a Defined Benefit pension. The risk has shifted from the employer to the employee. You are now the Pension Fund Manager of 'You, Inc.' This means you must accumulate the assets, manage the risk, and determine the payout rate. This guide explains how to construct a reliable income stream from a pile of 401(k) and IRA assets.

Key Takeaways

  • The 4% Rule: The modern pension. If you have $1 Million saved, you can withdraw $40,000/year (adjusted for inflation) with a high probability of the money lasting 30 years.
  • Social Security as the Floor: Think of Social Security as your 'Base Pension.' It is inflation-protected and guaranteed. Your savings only need to cover the gap between Social Security and your expenses.
  • SPIA (Single Premium Immediate Annuity): You can literally buy a pension. You give an insurance company a lump sum (e.g., $200k) and they guarantee you a monthly check for life. Useful for risk-averse retirees.
  • Dividend Growth: A portfolio of Dividend Aristocrats can act as a growing pension, providing cash flow that rises faster than inflation.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The shift to Defined Contribution (401k) plans means 'Longevity Risk' (living too long) is your problem. In a pension, if you live to 105, the company pays. In a 401(k), if you live to 105, you might run out of money. Hedging this tail risk is the primary goal of modern retirement planning.

Constructing the Paycheck

You need to turn a pile of cash into a monthly stream.

Layer 1: Guaranteed Income (The Floor)

Goal: Cover 'Needs' (Housing, Food, Utilities).
Sources: Social Security + Buying an Annuity (SPIA).
Strategy: If your needs are $4,000/mo and Social Security covers $2,500, consider buying a small annuity to cover the remaining $1,500. This ensures you never starve, regardless of the stock market.

Layer 2: Portfolio Drawdown (The Lifestyle)

Goal: Cover 'Wants' (Travel, Dining, Hobbies).
Source: 401(k) / IRA withdrawals.
Strategy: Use the 4% Rule. If the market crashes, you can cut back on 'Wants' (skip the cruise) to preserve capital. This flexibility protects the portfolio.

Layer 3: Cash Buffer (The Shock Absorber)

Goal: Avoid selling stocks in a crash.
Source: 2 years of expenses in Cash/T-Bills.
Strategy: When the market is down, spend the cash. When the market is up, sell stocks to refill the cash bucket.

The 'Bucket' Strategy

  1. Bucket 1 (Years 1-3): Cash & Short-Term Bonds. Safe, liquid. Pays the bills now.
  2. Bucket 2 (Years 4-10): Intermediate Bonds & Dividend Stocks. Moderate growth/income.
  3. Bucket 3 (Years 11+): Total Stock Market Index. High growth to beat inflation for your 80s and 90s.
  4. The Refill: Once a year, move money from Bucket 3 -> Bucket 2 -> Bucket 1 to keep the conveyor belt moving.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are annuities bad?

Expensive 'Variable Annuities' are often bad (high fees). Simple 'Immediate Annuities' (SPIA) are good tools. You trade a lump sum for a guaranteed paycheck. It is insurance against living too long.

What if the 4% rule fails?

The 4% rule assumes you never adjust spending. If you are flexible (e.g., spend less in bad years), the success rate jumps to nearly 100%. Flexibility is the ultimate safety net.

How much do I need?

Multiply your annual 'Gap' (Expenses minus Social Security) by 25. Example: Need $40k extra/year -> $1 Million Portfolio.
